With December just around the corner I want to remind you to get your
entries in for our show at the Port Moody Arts Centre. We need a lot of pieces to
make the show a success. You need to submit a photo of your pieces to Ed Pretty
ASAP so we can go ahead with the jurying process. The theme is ‘Not Just Round’
which encompasses everything we turn. This will be a great place for us to show (and
sell if you want) our work. Let’s put on a good showing.
I am looking forward to Derek Weidman coming January 3rd and 4th for a
demo and class. Derek’s turnings are mind boggling! I don’t know how he makes the
things he does on the lathe. Even though I am a beginner turner I am going to try and
get a seat in his class. Not only will I learn a lot at the demo, but there is nothing like
getting hands on instruction from world class demonstrators, no matter what level of
turning you are at. Derek is one I have to see.
Want to be our next newsletter editor? Ron the current editor is stepping
down and has agreed to help the new editor with the next edition so it will be a
smooth transition. The newsletter is one of the big benefits of being a Guild member.
Not only is it filled with information and interesting articles but it is an important
part of our communications. I for one look forward to reading it each month and
catching up on things I missed. If you are interested in the position, please talk to
Ron or me for more info. And thanks to Ron for all the hard work.
The Ice Scream dedication at David Lede House (Canuck Place Abbotsford)
went well. About two dozen people were in attendance including some of the
original turners. Karina Chow was a gracious hostess offering us refreshments and a
private tour of the facility. Look for an article in this or the next newsletter about
the event. Thanks to David Sweet and Karina for putting this all together.
Alan Cusworth is going to teach us how to make a wedding goblet at this
month’s meeting. I am hoping he will include turning the captured ring. I have always
wanted to try one of those.
We don’t have a meeting next month as it is Christmas. Or next meeting is
January 28th, so please remember Derek Weidman’s class and demo Jan 3 & 4.
Have a very merry Christmas, and a great New Year!
Happy Turning.
Bill

Volume 16, Issue 9 November 2014

One of the mandates of our Guild is to promote the Craft and Art of woodturning and a great way to do that is to
put on a show where the public can see what we do. Anyone who has helped out at our Brentwood Show will know how
excited people get when they see our stuff. Yet, it has been a while since we have had and exhibition in a gallery. Recently, a chance came up to have a show at the Port Moody Arts Centre in January 2015. The idea is that all of us can have
a chance to show off what we do in a month-long show in a gallery that promotes its shows through web sites, posters,
rack cards, an opening reception, and lots of social media. The Opening Reception (on a Thursday evening) usually gets
over 150 visitors.
When Janice Cotter, Gallery Curator asked me for a name for the show I suggested “Not Just Round” – a way for
us to all think outside the “circle”. She then asked who would jury the show. I suggested that she be one juror, that she
pick someone from the local art community and that I would ask well-known Canadian turner Michael Hosaluk to be the
other juror. I am pleased to say he has accepted.
So, here is how the process works:
• There is no cost to you to enter. The Guild will pay the hanging fees.
• Take good high-resolution pictures of your pieces – one per piece
• Prepare the stats of each piece – height and diameter (or width and depth), material, finish, price (NFS is OK)
• Prepare a short explanation of how you think the piece meets the theme of the show. It doesn’t have to be
fancy but sometimes the jury likes to know your intentions. If you have several pieces that are similar then one
statement is enough.
• Send all that to me at bvcampbell@telus.net by end-of-day December 8th,2014. I will take all the entries and
make up a “blind” list. The jury members will see the pictures, statistics, and your statement but not your
name. They will decide which pieces to select and let us know by late December.
• Those that are selected will be sent a contract that tells you what is expected from you and what the Gallery
will do for you. It also ensures that your work remains your property until it is sold (if you make it for sale) or until
it is returned to you.
• I know that Janice wants lots of pieces ( 150 or more) and she wants variety – big, small, things that hang on
the wall, pieces that hang from the ceiling, etc. So be imaginative and enter lots of pieces.
The idea of entering a juried show can be intimidating and there are lots of reasons why people may not want to
enter. Here are a few I have heard or said to myself:
• I can’t think of an idea.
• I’m not an artist.
• My stuff is not good enough.
•
No one will like this
•
What if I don’t get accepted?
•
Only our best turners should do that
•
I never sell my stuff so why bother?
To all that I want to say “Humbug” or words to that effect. We always see our mistakes and flaws while nonturners only see the magnificent work that they cannot image could be handmade. Also, it is very rewarding to be part of
a show and to see what goes on behind the scenes.
Please plan to enter the show and if you have questions of concerns let me know. I would be happy to chat.
Should I enter the “Not Just Round” show? - Bruce Campbell

Improving both workshop environment and community relations at the same time.
Those members of the guild who have participated in “hands on” workshops, both visiting demonstrators and/or 101 sessions, will be familiar with the excellent facility made available to us by KMS tools. What everyone may not know is that KMS provides this fully equipped classroom at no cost to the guild.
The guild executive is very pleased to advise everyone that, as a token of the guild’s appreciation to KMS, and in order to
enhance the facility even further, we have purchased, donated and installed a dust filtration system in the KMS classroom.
This action came as the result of discussions during the course of an executive meeting that resulted in a request to Barry
Wilkinson and Ed Pretty to research the matter and make a proposal. The subsequent proposal led to the executive approving the
action and the new clean air system was installed in the workshop in October by Barry Wilkinson, assisted by Bob Askew.
The new clean air system, which can be seen in the photograph, will make the workshop experience even safer and more
comfortable for both guild members and other users of the facility. An added benefit of this donation is that it provides the guild the
opportunity to promote ourselves to potential new members who we need to both sustain and grow our community.
A second promotion with KMS will commence at the same time where purchasers of new lathes at the KMS Coquitlam
store will receive a certificate with the lathe entitling them to one year’s free membership of the guild.
Donation of Air Cleaner to KMS Tools - Bob Askew

Making a teapot is a good challenge for a woodturner. Woodturning is a subtractive art; we remove parts of a log leaving
only our finished object. Teapots need a body, a handle, a spout, a lid, and (often) a foot. Although this could be done as a purely
subtractive process, it’s more likely that we would choose to make several turned objects and join them together. Many
woodturners also do “flat” woodwork and are familiar with joining pieces, but joining turned objects presents some new challenges.
I’ll leave the discussion of joining these objects for another article.
Consider the teapot body. Many hollow forms would make good teapot bodies, but what if you don't make hollow forms?
A simple alternative would be to make two bowls of the same diameter and then glue them together at the rims to form a hollow
object. In my demo, I showed a variation of this idea that yields a more asymmetric vessel.
Begin with a spindle blank measuring about 3” square and 6” long. Mount it between centers and turn tenons on both ends
to fit the chuck, leaving the rest of the blank square. Remove the blank from the lathe and draw a line across one face of the blank at
about 10 degrees off perpendicular to the axis of rotation and a bit off center (lengthwise). Using a bandsaw, cut along that line and
then sand both of the exposed surfaces flat (using a belt sander or disc sander). The two blanks are slightly different sized. The larger one will be used to make the top of the teapot body and the smaller one will be used for the bottom of the teapot body.
Mount the larger (top) blank in the chuck. Using a drill bit mounted in the tail stock, drill a 1/2” diameter hole about 1”
deep. Remove this piece from the chuck and repeat the process with the smaller (bottom) blank, drilling the 1/2” diameter hole only
about 1/2” deep.
Leaving the smaller blank in the chuck, push a 1/2” dowel about 1 1/4” long into the drilled hole. Push the larger blank onto
this dowel matching the angles of the cut ends. Bring up the tail stock and add a bit of pressure so that the entire assemblage can be
turned.
Shape the outside of piece, bearing in mind where the cut starts and ends. I made a sort of egg shape, with the largest
diameter in the area of the cut. Leave the ends unshaped, leaving enough material to provide support when excavating the insides of
the bowls. Sand as required.
Back off the tail stock, remove the larger blank and the dowel and leaving the smaller blank mounted in the chuck. Make an
end grain bowl (with angled rim) out of the smaller blank. This can be done using a bowl gouge, a spindle gouge, or other tools, as
you prefer. In the demo, I used a parting tool to produce a flat surface from the dowel hole out to the angled rim and then used a
Jackofsky hollower to remove the rest of the wood. Whatever tool you use, leave the wall thickness about 1/4” at the rim. (It can
be thinner away from the rim if you’d prefer.) There is no need to sand the inside. Be sure to leave the bottom of the bowl thick as
it will be sanded later to form a foot that is not square to this orientation of the bowl. Shape and sand the lower portion of the bowl
and then part it off.
Mount the larger blank in the chuck and repeat the process, leaving the rim about 1/4” and untouched. Before parting off,
drill a 3/4" hole into waste wood in chuck, creating a hole for the teapot lid. Part off revealing this hole.
The next task is to join the two parts of the teapot body together. Lightly coat each rim with standard wood glue. Align the two
rims so that they are about 180 degrees off of the original alignment,
creating a bend at the seam. Press the two parts together and rotate
back and forth, squeezing out some glue. As you continue to rub the
parts together, there will be more and more resistance. As it becomes
difficult to move the parts, make sure that the parts are properly
aligned and then set it aside to dry for 24 hours.
Once dried, you can sand around the joint to create a smooth
curve rather than an angle at the glue joint line. Next, sand a flat on the
bottom so that the vessel sits with both top and bottom of vessel oriented away from vertical. Now, all to need to do is to make the spout,
handle, and lid. We’ll leave that for a future demo.
Making a teapot body with a twist - Art Liestman

Canuck Place Children’s Hospice was excited to have members of the Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild donate a unique and whimsical piece that was collaboratively crafted to inspire smiles,
wonder, and enjoyment of the children at its new Abbotsford location – Dave Lede House.
Approximately fourteen GVWG members attended the donation ceremony on site at Dave Lede
House on Saturday, November 1, 2014 at 2:00 p.m. GVWG President Bill Fowle made the donation on behalf
of the Guild to Karina Chow, Manager of Development for Canuck Place Fraser Region. Bill provided insights
about the history of the Guild, its importance as a friendly and interactive place for woodturners, and about
the wooden art piece called I SCREAM! that was the vision of Larry Stevenson and crafted by 30 GVWG
collaborators in 2003 for the American Association of Woodturners symposium in Pasadena, CA. In turn,
Karina provided information about the significant work of the Children’s Hospice, the large numbers of
affected families and their loved ones that need care, and how it is anticipated that this turned sculpture will
bring great joy to all that see it at the hospice. Karina thanked the Guild for its generosity and insights and then took the members
on a private tour of the soon-to-open Dave Lede House.
Canuck Place Children’s Hospice is British Columbia’s recognized pediatric palliative care provider. Over 560 newborns,
children and teens with life-threatening illnesses and their families receive care from CPCH through outreach programs and two
provincial hospice locations in Vancouver and Abbotsford. Services include clinical respite and family support, pain and symptom
management, 24-hour phone consultation support and in-house clinical care, art and education, recreation therapy, grief and loss
counselling, and end-of-life care. Through the investment of the community, Canuck Place Children’s Hospice’s talented team and
over 325 energetic volunteers make a lasting difference in the lives of children and the families who love them.
The I SCREAM! award-winning sculpture is now installed on the main floor of Dave Lede House adjacent to the volunteer
office. Canuck Place is grateful to community groups such as the GVWG for donations that will enliven the experience of its families
and provide joy to the children who are on the care program.
For more information, or to learn how you can become involved, go to www.canuckplace.org

This year Focus on Fundamentals will be concentrating on the basic features of bowl turning. Our first presenter for the
season was Gerry Vickers. Gerry is a longstanding member of GVWG and a great teacher. He is the coordinator of Turning 101
which takes place monthly. As with the beginning of all FOF sessions Gerry talked about the safety guidelines for turning and emphasized the importance of a face shield.
We started the session by talking about how to approach a piece of wood and what characteristics to look for in making
your bowl blank. Gerry’s presentation was called “Bowl Basic Fixing”. He focused on how to ‘fix’ the blank to the head stock in
preparation for turning. He first talked about the wood worm. You have to decide what side of the blank will be the inside of the
bowl as with the wood worm you will waste some material due to the depth of the screw which is usually about one inch. You use a
drill bit a little smaller than the wood worm and drill a hole. Gerry uses his drill press as he has more control and it is safer. Next,
with the lathe off, you put the wood worm in your chuck and feed the blank onto the wood worm being sure it is tight to the jaws of
the chuck. Bring up the tail stock and for safety lock it. Adjust the tool rest to the height you want to turn and by hand turn the
blank to ensure it clears the tool rest. Before you start the lathe adjust the speed to the lowest speed, stand off to the side to ensure your own safety in case the blank is not secure, and adjust the speed up to the speed you feel comfortable for turning.
Next, Gerry talked about how to attach a blank to the lathe using a face plate. You need a fairly flat surface and again there
will be some waste where the screws go into the blank so plan wisely. Gerry showed us several methods of finding the center of
the blank. He uses regular wood screws as other screws such as gyproc and masonry screws are brittle and tend to break. With the
face plate attached to the blank, screw the face plate onto the head stock. Again, be sure to bring up the tail stock and lock it for
safety. Position the tool rest, ensure there is clearance from the blank and start the lathe at the lowest speed, gradually increasing to
your level of comfort.
We then talked about shaping the bottom of the
bowl and the methods of making the foot, either expansion
or compression tenon. Gerry also spent a few minutes
demonstrating the use of the Cole Jaws for finishing the
bottom of the bowl.
There was good discussion throughout the demonstration.
We thank Gerry for providing such an informative talk.
